open_questions: Is the token-level dependency parsing failure due to task formulation mismatch (token-level vs. component-level granularity), sequence length sensitivity, search space complexity, insufficient training data, or inherent unsuitability of parsing for AM? Component-level dependency parsing baseline would clarify whether failure is specific to token-level formulation or general to parsing approaches.

Do the findings (model rankings, distance-encoding effectiveness, length-invariance, MTL benefits) generalize to other argumentation corpora with different structural properties (Peldszus & Stede 2016 microtexts, legal documents, scientific papers)? Cross-dataset evaluation is essential for assessing generalizability beyond PE dataset.

Are the MTL improvements (~5% C-F1) statistically significant and practically meaningful? Significance testing and confidence intervals would clarify whether improvements are reliable or within typical variance ranges for neural training.

How much of STagBLCC's performance improvement comes from the character-level CNN vs. the tagging framework itself? Ablation study comparing STagBLCC (with CNN) to STagBL (without CNN) would isolate the contribution of each component.

Could LSTM-ER's essay-level degradation be fixed by adapting TreeLSTM to operate on document-level structures rather than sentence-level? Document-level TreeLSTM variant or alternative relation modeling would clarify whether degradation is inherent to decoupling or fixable with architectural adaptation.

Would neural methods still outperform the ILP baseline if both were evaluated under equal information conditions (essay-level only, without paragraph-level information)? Re-evaluation of ILP without paragraph advantage would isolate the contribution of neural methods vs. feature-based methods.

Is the length-invariance property of local models due to inherent properties of tagging (every subsequence forms valid input) or due to other factors (smaller search space, explicit distance encoding bias, different training data)? Controlled experiment varying sequence length while holding other factors constant would directly test the length-invariance claim.

Do the distance-encoding scheme and model rankings depend on the specific distance distribution of the PE dataset? Analysis of distance distributions in other corpora and evaluation of whether distance encoding needs to be adapted would assess generalizability of the approach.

Recommend acceptance with major revisions addressing: (1) cross-dataset evaluation on Peldszus & Stede (2016) microtexts or other corpora to assess generalization; (2) fair comparisons with equal training conditions (essay-level parser training or paragraph-level tagger training) and equal information access (ILP without paragraph advantage); (3) ablation studies isolating CNN contribution and statistical significance testing for MTL improvements; (4) component-level parsing baseline to clarify whether parsing failure is due to task formulation or inherent unsuitability. Alternatively, accept as-is with explicit acknowledgment of limitations and framing of conclusions as PE-dataset-specific findings that require cross-dataset validation before claiming generalizability. The paper's honest reporting of negative results and mechanistic analysis are commendable and should be preserved in any revision.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Strengths to emphasize: (1) First neural end-to-end AM solutions with systematic comparison across four framings; (2) Non-obvious negative result (token-level parsing fails) challenges intuitive assumptions and provides mechanistic explanation; (3) Distance-encoding label scheme is a practical innovation enabling local models to capture relation information; (4) Honest reporting of negative results and modest MTL improvements; (5) Mechanistic analysis (Figure 4, O(2m²) explanation) goes beyond reporting numbers. Critical limitations to address: (1) Single-dataset evaluation—conduct cross-dataset evaluation on Peldszus & Stede (2016) microtexts or other corpora to assess whether findings hold; (2) Confounded comparisons—either train parsers on essay level (addressing memory constraints with gradient checkpointing, smaller batches) or train taggers on paragraph level for fair comparison; (3) Statistical significance testing—report p-values and confidence intervals for MTL improvements and neural vs. ILP comparisons; (4) Ablation studies—isolate CNN contribution to STagBLCC and clarify whether tagging superiority is due to formulation or architecture; (5) Alternative explanations—test component-level dependency parsing to clarify whether failure is due to token-level granularity mismatch or inherent unsuitability of parsing; (6) Generalizability of distance encoding—analyze distance distributions in other corpora and discuss how encoding would need to be adapted. Specific revisions: (1) Reframe dependency parsing failure claim as 'token-level dependency parsing is ineffective' rather than 'dependency parsing is ineffective' to acknowledge task formulation specificity; (2) Acknowledge ILP information advantage and discuss implications for neural vs. feature-based comparison; (3) Provide learning curves showing performance as function of sequence length and training data to support length-invariance and data efficiency claims; (4) Discuss practical implications of paragraph-level vs. essay-level results and when each is actionable; (5) Acknowledge that distance-encoding scheme is task-specific and may not generalize to corpora with different distance distributions.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper presents the first neural end-to-end solutions to computational argumentation mining, systematically comparing four neural framings (dependency parsing, sequence tagging, multi-task learning, LSTM-ER) on the Stab & Gurevych (2016) PE dataset. The core contributions are: (1) empirical evidence that neural end-to-end AM outperforms feature-based ILP baselines (60.46% vs 44.68% F1 on essays); (2) a non-obvious negative result showing token-level dependency parsing fails dramatically despite tree-like argument structures (32.84% vs 49.87% C-F1); (3) a practical distance-encoding label scheme enabling sequence tagging to jointly model components and relations; (4) mechanistic analysis explaining why simpler local models outperform complex global models across document scales. The paper is well-executed within its scope, with honest reporting of negative results and detailed mechanistic explanations. However, significant methodological limitations constrain confidence in generalizability: single-dataset evaluation prevents cross-corpus validation; confounded comparisons weaken causal claims; lack of statistical significance testing for key comparisons; and alternative explanations for observed phenomena remain plausible.

Strengths:
1. First systematic neural end-to-end AM comparison across four distinct framings with consistent evaluation metrics and honest reporting of negative results
2. Non-obvious negative result (token-level dependency parsing fails despite tree-like structures) challenges intuitive assumptions and provides mechanistic explanations (search space complexity, sequence length)
3. Novel distance-encoding label scheme (Eq. 1) is a practical task-specific innovation enabling sequence tagging to jointly model components and relations while biasing toward realistic distance distributions
4. Mechanistic analysis goes beyond reporting numbers: Figure 4 shows distance preference differences between models; O(2m²) explanation for LSTM-ER degradation; length-invariance property of local models
5. Robust performance of STagBLCC across document scales (only ~5% R-F1 drop paragraph→essay vs ~26% for parsers) demonstrates practical value for real-world deployment
6. Evaluation at multiple granularities (exact 100% and approximate 50% span matching) reveals different model rankings and systematic span prediction errors
7. Clear presentation of task formulation, data structure, and design choices enables reproducibility and understanding of why certain architectural decisions were made
8. Honest acknowledgment of limitations: ILP information advantage (line 750), paragraph-level parser training constraint (line 605), modest MTL improvements (lines 690-695)

Limitations:
1. Single-dataset evaluation (PE only, 402 essays, 80 test) severely limits generalization claims; no cross-dataset evaluation on Peldszus & Stede (2016) microtexts or other argumentation corpora with different structural properties; dataset-specific properties may drive model choices and conclusions about which framing is 'best'
2. Dependency parsers trained only on paragraph level due to memory constraints (line 605) while tagging models trained on essay level creates confound; LSTM-Parser's essay-level performance (32.84% C-F1) is from paragraph-trained model tested on longer sequences, making it unclear whether failure is due to task formulation mismatch, insufficient training data, or inherent unsuitability of parsing
3. ILP baseline has access to more information (paragraph + essay level) than neural systems (essay level only), giving ILP unfair advantage; authors acknowledge this (line 750) but do not re-evaluate ILP under equal information conditions; paragraph-level comparison shows ILP and STagBLCC nearly identical (55.23% vs 55.22%), undermining superiority claim at that scale
4. No statistical significance testing for key comparisons: MTL improvements (~5% C-F1) lack significance testing despite being modest; neural vs. ILP comparisons lack significance testing; only within-neural comparisons report Wilcoxon test (p < 0.01)
5. Character-level CNN contribution to STagBLCC performance is unclear; no ablation study isolates CNN component; STagBL (without CNN) is ~10% lower than STagBLCC (with CNN) in C-F1 exact match, but unclear whether improvement comes from CNN or CRF label dependencies
6. Distance-encoding assumption (finite, discrete distances with ~2/3 of relations in {-2,-1,1}) may not generalize to other argumentation corpora with different distance distributions or relation types; no cross-dataset validation of distance distribution assumption

Open Questions:
1. Is the token-level dependency parsing failure due to task formulation mismatch (token-level vs. component-level granularity), sequence length sensitivity, search space complexity, insufficient training data, or inherent unsuitability of parsing for AM? Component-level dependency parsing baseline would clarify whether failure is specific to token-level formulation or general to parsing approaches.
2. Do the findings (model rankings, distance-encoding effectiveness, length-invariance, MTL benefits) generalize to other argumentation corpora with different structural properties (Peldszus & Stede 2016 microtexts, legal documents, scientific papers)? Cross-dataset evaluation is essential for assessing generalizability beyond PE dataset.
3. Are the MTL improvements (~5% C-F1) statistically significant and practically meaningful? Significance testing and confidence intervals would clarify whether improvements are reliable or within typical variance ranges for neural training.
4. How much of STagBLCC's performance improvement comes from the character-level CNN vs. the tagging framework itself? Ablation study comparing STagBLCC (with CNN) to STagBL (without CNN) would isolate the contribution of each component.
5. Could LSTM-ER's essay-level degradation be fixed by adapting TreeLSTM to operate on document-level structures rather than sentence-level? Document-level TreeLSTM variant or alternative relation modeling would clarify whether degradation is inherent to decoupling or fixable with architectural adaptation.
6. Would neural methods still outperform the ILP baseline if both were evaluated under equal information conditions (essay-level only, without paragraph-level information)? Re-evaluation of ILP without paragraph advantage would isolate the contribution of neural methods vs. feature-based methods.
7. Is the length-invariance property of local models due to inherent properties of tagging (every subsequence forms valid input) or due to other factors (smaller search space, explicit distance encoding bias, different training data)? Controlled experiment varying sequence length while holding other factors constant would directly test the length-invariance claim.
8. Do the distance-encoding scheme and model rankings depend on the specific distance distribution of the PE dataset? Analysis of distance distributions in other corpora and evaluation of whether distance encoding needs to be adapted would assess generalizability of the approach.

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about design choices and limitations, but several key gaps limit confidence in generalizability and causal mechanisms. The paper honestly reports negative results and provides mechanistic explanations, which strengthens credibility. However, the paper acknowledges but does not address the ILP information advantage and paragraph-level parser training constraint, creating transparency gaps about fairness of comparisons. The paper does not provide statistical significance testing for key comparisons (MTL improvements, neural vs. ILP), ablation studies for design choices (CNN contribution, distance encoding effectiveness), or discussion of generalization to other corpora. These transparency gaps limit confidence in the robustness and generalizability of the findings. The paper's clear presentation of task formulation, data structure, and mechanistic analysis are commendable and should be preserved in any revision.

This article is published with open access at Springerlink.com Abstract In this article the argumentation structure of the court’s decision in the Popov v. Hayashi case is formalised in Prakken’s (Argument Comput 1:93–124; 2010) abstract framework for argument-based inference with structured arguments. In this framework, arguments are inference trees formed by applying two kinds of inference rules, strict and defeasible rules. Arguments can be attacked in three ways: attacking a premise, attacking a conclusion and attacking an inference. To resolve such conﬂicts, preferences may be used, which leads to three corresponding kinds of defeat, after which Dung’s (Artif Intell 77:321–357; 1995) abstract acceptability semantics can be used to evaluate the arguments. In the present paper the abstract framework is instantiated with strict inference rules corresponding to ﬁrst-order logic and with defeasible inference rules for defeasible modus ponens and various argument schemes. The main techniques used in the formal reconstruction of the case are rule-exception structures and arguments about rule validity. Arguments about socio-legal values and the use of precedent cases are reduced to arguments about rule validity. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Reconstructing Popov v. Hayashi in a framework for argumentation with structured arguments and Dungean semantics
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Reconstructing Popov v. Hayashi in a framework for argumentation with structured arguments and Dungean semantics Henry Prakken Published online: 11 March 2012 /C211 The Author(s) 2012. This article is published with open access at Springerlink.com Abstract In this article the argumentation structure of the court’s decision in the Popov v. Hayashi case is formalised in Prakken’s (Argument Comput 1:93–124; 2010) abstract framework for argument-based inference with structured arguments. In this framework, arguments are inference trees formed by applying two kinds of inference rules, strict and defeasible rules. Arguments can be attacked in three ways: attacking a premise, attacking a conclusion and attacking an inference. To resolve such conﬂicts, preferences may be used, which leads to three corresponding kinds of defeat, after which Dung’s (Artif Intell 77:321–357; 1995) abstract acceptability semantics can be used to evaluate the arguments. In the present paper the abstract framework is instantiated with strict inference rules corresponding to ﬁrst-order logic and with defeasible inference rules for defeasible modus ponens and various argument schemes. The main techniques used in the formal reconstruction of the case are rule-exception structures and arguments about rule validity. Arguments about socio-legal values and the use of precedent cases are reduced to arguments about rule validity. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
